results.question: Do creatures phasing back in trigger enter the battlefield abilities?
results.text: No. When a permanent phases in, that is not an “enter the battlefield” event and so it doesn’t cause enters-the-battlefield (ETB) triggered abilities to trigger. Phasing is a static ability that changes how the untap step works: during the untap step phased-in permanents phase out and phased-out permanents that phased out under that player’s control phase in (see [702.26a] and [502.1]). Phased-in permanents are simply treated as though they exist again when they phase in ([702.26c]), but phasing does not move a permanent between zones or change control, and zone-change triggers don’t trigger when a permanent phases in or out ([702.26d]). Enters-the-battlefield abilities are zone-change triggers (they trigger when a permanent enters the battlefield) ([603.6a] and [603.6c]), so they won’t trigger from a phasing-in. Note that the rules do make a specific exception for abilities that trigger when a permanent phases out (those look back in time) ([603.10b]); that exception does not make phasing in into an ETB event. Assumption: this answer applies the default two-player and multiplayer rules shown here; nothing in the provided rules makes phasing-in cause ETB triggers in any player-count case.

results.question: how does trample work with deathtouch?
results.text:
Short answer: When an attacking creature with trample also has deathtouch, you need only assign one point of damage to each blocking creature (a nonzero amount) for that creature to count as having been assigned lethal damage; any remaining damage can be assigned to the defending player or planeswalker as allowed by trample. After damage is dealt, any creature dealt damage by a source with deathtouch and with toughness > 0 is destroyed as a state‑based action.

What “deathtouch” means here: deathtouch makes any nonzero amount of damage dealt by that source count as lethal for the purpose of determining whether excess damage is being dealt (definition used for trample assignment) [702.2c].

What “trample” means here: trample changes how an attacking creature assigns combat damage: the controller first assigns what’s needed to give each blocking creature lethal damage, and only after that may assign excess to the defending player or planeswalker (assignment must take into account damage already marked on those creatures and damage being assigned at the same time) [702.19a, 702.19b, 120.6]. Because deathtouch changes what counts as lethal, a trampling creature with deathtouch needs to assign only a nonzero amount (normally 1) to each blocker to satisfy the ‘‘lethal’’ requirement; any further damage is ‘‘excess’’ and can be assigned to the player/planeswalker [702.2c, 120.4a, 702.19b].

Planeswalker note: for trample over planeswalkers, you must assign lethal damage to blockers and damage at least equal to the planeswalker’s loyalty before assigning further excess elsewhere; deathtouch still reduces the lethal amount required for the blocking creatures to one point each, but you must also satisfy the planeswalker’s loyalty requirement where applicable [702.19c, 120.4a].

After damage is dealt: damage dealt by a source with deathtouch causes creatures dealt nonzero damage by that source to be destroyed as state‑based actions (assuming toughness > 0) when SBA are checked; damage marked remains until cleanup (or regeneration) [702.2b, 704.5h, 120.6].

Assumptions: I assumed the normal combat damage assignment timing (attacker assigns then blocker assigns) and a two‑player situation attacking a player unless a planeswalker was specified; the answer’s core point (only 1 assigned damage needed per blocker when the trampling source has deathtouch) is the same in multiplayer but the identity of the ‘‘defending player(s)’’ could affect where excess damage may be assigned [702.19b].

results.question: is storm a triggered ability that can be countered?
results.text:
Yes. Storm is a triggered ability that functions on the stack, and the storm ability itself can only be countered by effects that counter abilities (not by effects that counter only spells).

Definitions and rules applied
- Triggered ability: “Triggered abilities have a trigger condition and an effect. They are written as ‘[When/Whenever/At] [trigger condition or event], [effect].’ ” [603.1a]
- Storm: “Storm is a triggered ability that functions on the stack. ‘When you cast this spell, copy it for each other spell that was cast before it this turn. If the spell has any targets, you may choose new targets for any of the copies.’ ” This establishes that storm is a triggered ability and that it goes on the stack when it triggers. [702.40a]
- Triggering and placement on the stack: When the storm trigger condition is met (you cast the spell), the ability triggers automatically and is put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority. The ability on the stack remains there until it resolves or is countered. [603.2a] [603.3]
- Countering: “Activated and triggered abilities on the stack aren’t spells, and therefore can’t be countered by anything that counters only spells. Activated and triggered abilities on the stack can be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities.” So a storm triggered ability can't be countered by a generic “counter target spell” effect, but it can be countered by a card or effect that explicitly says it counters abilities. [113.9]

Practical consequence: when you cast a spell that has storm, the storm trigger is put on the stack. That storm trigger can be removed from the stack only by resolving, being countered by an effect that counters abilities, or otherwise being removed by a rule or effect; it cannot be countered by effects that only counter spells. [702.40a] [603.3] [113.9]

Assumptions and scope
- I assume the provided rules are the complete context; no specific card text that modifies or overrides storm was given. If a particular card’s text said its storm ability “can’t be countered,” that card text would override the general rule (card text overrides general rules).

results.question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?
results.text:
No. If a card has a two-color hybrid mana symbol in its mana cost or rules text (for example {R/G}), that card’s color identity includes both colors and it can only be in a commander deck whose commander’s color identity contains both of those colors; it can’t be put into a deck whose commander has only one of those colors (see rules [903.5c] and [903.4f]).

Definitions and explanation
- Color identity: the color or colors of any mana symbols in a card’s mana cost or rules text (plus any colors from characteristic-defining abilities or a color indicator) (see [903.4f] and [202.2d]).
- Hybrid mana symbol: a mana symbol that represents a cost that can be paid in one of two ways; a hybrid symbol is all of its component colors (see [107.4e]).

Practical consequences
- A card with a {R/G} hybrid symbol has both red and green in its color identity, so it can’t be included in a mono-red or mono-green commander deck—its commander must have both red and green in its color identity ([107.4e], [903.4f], [903.5c]).
- A monocolored hybrid symbol such as {2/W} has only the colored component (white) as its color, so a card with only {2/W} (and no other colored symbols) has white in its color identity and could be included in a white-only commander deck ([107.4e], [202.2d], [903.5c]).

Assumptions: I’m answering for the standard Commander deck-construction rules; this outcome doesn’t change depending on player count.

results.question: can I respond to the untap step?
results.text:
No. You cannot respond during the untap step. No player receives priority during the untap step, so you can’t cast spells or activate abilities while the untap actions are happening; the untap actions are turn‑based and don’t use the stack. Any abilities that trigger during the untap step are held and put on the stack when the upkeep begins (before the active player gets priority).

Definitions and brief reasons:
- “Respond” here means casting spells or activating (and resolving) abilities in reaction to things happening; that requires having priority (see below) [117.1].
- Priority: the right to cast spells, activate abilities, and take special actions; the active player normally receives priority at the start of most steps, but no player receives priority during the untap step [117.1][117.3a].
- The untap actions (choosing which permanents untap and untapping them) are turn‑based actions that don’t use the stack, so nothing can be put on the stack in response to them [502.3].
- Phasing is a static ability that modifies the untap step: phased‑in permanents phase out and phased‑out permanents phase in as part of the untap turn‑based actions; those actions also don’t use the stack [702.26a][502.1].
- Because no player receives priority during the untap step, triggered abilities that trigger there are held and put onto the stack at the beginning of the upkeep before the active player gets priority [502.4][503.1a].

This is the same in multiplayer and two‑player games—the untap step’s lack of priority applies regardless of player count.

Assumptions: none beyond the rules you provided; I assumed the ordinary sequence where untap step actions occur and any triggers from those actions would be handled at upkeep as described.

results.question: are creatures still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step?
results.text:
Yes. An attacking creature remains an attacking creature during the end of combat step. By definition, an Attacking Creature “remains an attacking creature until it’s removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first” ([Attacking Creature]). The end of combat step is part of the combat phase, and creatures are only removed from combat as soon as the end of combat step ends ([511.3]). Therefore creatures are still attacking during the entire end of combat step unless they were removed from combat earlier (for example, because they left the battlefield, their controller changed, they phased out, or another effect specifically removed them from combat) — see the list of things that remove a permanent from combat ([506.4]). Note also that “at end of combat” abilities trigger as the end of combat step begins and effects that last “until end of combat” don’t expire until the combat phase ends ([511.2]; [500.5a]). If an effect ends the combat phase (for example, Mandate of Peace), the combat phase can end without a normal end of combat step and “at end of combat” triggers won’t trigger in that case ([724.2d]; [724.2e]). Assumption: standard turn flow (no premature ending of the combat phase); multiplayer does not change this outcome under the provided rules.

Reasoning sources cited above show that the combat phase ends only when the end of combat step ends (or is skipped by a card effect), so creatures remain attacking during that step until removal or phase end.

results.question: Do you cast lands?
results.text:
No — you don’t cast lands. You play a land as a special action: to play a land is to put that land onto the battlefield from the zone it’s in (usually your hand). Playing a land is a special action that doesn’t use the stack, the land is never a spell, and players can’t respond to playing a land with instants or activated abilities. You may play a land only when you have priority during a main phase of your turn, the stack is empty, and you haven’t already played the number of lands you’re allowed this turn (normally one, unless a continuous effect increases it). Putting a land onto the battlefield by a spell or ability is not the same as playing a land. Artifact lands and any object that’s both a land and another card type still can only be played as lands and can’t be cast as spells.

Key definitions and points relied on:
- “To play a land” — put the land onto the battlefield from the zone it’s in (usually the hand). Playing a land is a special action. [701.18a] [Play] [116.2a]
- Playing a land doesn’t use the stack, is never a spell, and can’t be responded to. [305.1] [505.6b]
- You may play a land only during your main phase while you have priority and the stack is empty; you can’t play a land when it isn’t your turn. [305.1] [117.1] [305.3]
- Normally you may play one land per turn unless a continuous effect changes that. [305.2] [305.2b]
- Putting a land onto the battlefield (for example, via a spell or ability) is different from playing a land. [305.4]
- An object that’s both a land and another card type (for example, an artifact land) can only be played as a land and can’t be cast as a spell. [300.2a] [305.9] [Artifact Land]
- Lands normally have no mana cost and are played without paying any costs. [202.1b]

Assumptions: This answer uses the standard (two-player or multiplayer) rules as given; the cited rules apply the same way regardless of player count for this question.

results.question: can I sacrifice an evoked creature before that creature's evoke triggered ability resolves?
results.text:
Yes. Evoke creates a triggered ability that triggers when the permanent enters the battlefield ("When this permanent enters, if its evoke cost was paid, its controller sacrifices it"). That triggered ability is placed on the stack and will resolve later; you (or any player with the appropriate permission) can take actions in response while that trigger is waiting on the stack, including sacrificing the creature by another means. If the creature is no longer on the battlefield when the evoke trigger resolves, the trigger will still check its intervening "if" (the evoke cost check) and then attempt to make its controller sacrifice the permanent, but there will be nothing to sacrifice and the trigger will do nothing to that permanent.

Definitions and assumptions
- "Evoke": "Evoke [cost]" means you may cast the card for [cost] instead of its mana cost, and it grants a triggered ability that reads "When this permanent enters, if its evoke cost was paid, its controller sacrifices it." (rule [702.74a]).
- "Triggered ability": an ability that triggers when its event happens and then later resolves (see rules [603.7] and [602-style resolving references implied by 608.2a]).
- Assumption: normal timing and priority rules apply (i.e., the evoke triggered ability is put onto the stack and players get priority to act before it resolves). If an effect like one that ends the turn or ends the combat phase prevents triggered abilities from being put onto the stack (see rule [724.2a] for that kind of special process), that could change whether the evoke trigger is ever put onto the stack.

Relevant resolution notes
- The evoke sacrifice is a triggered ability that is checked and then resolves like other triggered abilities (rules [702.74a], [603.7], [608.2a]).
- You may take special actions any time you have priority (rule [116.2e]), so you may sacrifice the creature in response to the evoke trigger while that trigger is on the stack. 
- If the creature is gone when the evoke trigger resolves, the trigger's "if its evoke cost was paid" condition is checked and (if true) the trigger attempts to have you sacrifice that permanent; but you can't sacrifice a permanent that's not on the battlefield, so the trigger will simply have no effect on that permanent (compare the guidance about choosing to sacrifice during resolution when you control no creatures in rule [608.2d]).

results.question: if a card loses all abilities, does that include keyword abilities?
results.text:
Yes. If an effect causes an object to “lose all abilities,” that removes keyword abilities (for example, flying, trample, hexproof). 

Definition: A keyword ability is an ability whose name is printed as a keyword (a shorthand name for an ability), not extra printed rules text; see rule [702.1] and [702.1d].

Why: Keyword abilities are still abilities, so an effect that removes abilities removes them. Effects add or remove abilities (they cause an object to “gain” or “lose” abilities) per [113.10] and [113.10b]; removing an ability removes all instances of that ability ([113.10b]). Those kinds of ability-adding and ability-removing effects (and keyword counters) are applied together in layer 6 of the continuous-effects system ([613.1f]). Also, an effect that says an object “can’t have” a specified ability causes it to lose that ability and prevents it from gaining it ([113.11]).

results.question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?
results.text: Yes. Nothing in the provided rules forbids you from drawing while you already have your maximum hand size; maximum hand size only forces you to discard down during your cleanup step. See 402.2 (what “maximum hand size” means) and 514.1 / 703.4n (the turn-based action that discards excess cards at cleanup). Drawing itself is performed one card at a time (121.2), and an instruction to draw multiple cards is implemented as multiple individual draws (121.2 / 121.2b). If an effect explicitly says you can’t draw cards, you can’t draw even if you’re below or at your maximum (121.3 / 121.3a). Replacement effects that replace draws still apply even if your library is empty (121.6 / 121.6a / 614.11). If an effect moves cards from a library to a hand without using the word “draw,” those cards are not considered draws (121.5). Finally, if you are required to draw more cards than remain in your library, you draw as many as possible and then lose the game the next time a player would receive priority (104.3c). Assumption: I’m answering for ordinary game situations with no unusual rule variants; if a card or effect in the specific situation says otherwise, that card text would control (card text not provided here).

results.question: what happens when a planeswalker has 0 or less loyalty counters?
results.text:
Direct answer: If a planeswalker has 0 loyalty counters on it, it’s put into its owner’s graveyard as a state-based action. (This is stated explicitly by rule [704.5i] and repeated by rule [306.9].)

Definitions and reasoning:
- A counter is a marker placed on an object that modifies characteristics; the number of loyalty counters on a planeswalker indicates its loyalty ([122.1e]).
- A planeswalker’s loyalty on the battlefield equals the number of loyalty counters on it ([306.5c]; see also [209.1] about entering with loyalty counters).
- State-based actions are automatic game actions that happen whenever certain conditions are met and don’t use the stack ([704.1]). One of those state-based actions is that a planeswalker with loyalty 0 is put into its owner’s graveyard ([704.5i], [306.9]).
- Damage dealt to a planeswalker causes that many loyalty counters to be removed, which can cause the planeswalker’s loyalty to reach 0 and thus trigger the state-based action ([120.3c], [306.8]).

Assumption: The provided rules speak only of “loyalty 0” (not “less than 0”). I assume loyalty (the number of loyalty counters) is not intended to be negative; under that assumption “0 or less” reduces to “0,” and the quoted state-based action applies. The provided rules do not explicitly say what to do if an effect somehow produced a negative loyalty number, so I can’t cite a rule for that hypothetical beyond the statements above.

results.question: do non-creature artifacts die?
results.text:
No — a non-creature artifact does not “die.”

Definition and ruling: “Dies” means “is put into a graveyard from the battlefield,” and that term applies to a creature or planeswalker (see [Dies] and [700.4]). Because that definition names only a creature or a planeswalker, an object that is only an artifact (i.e., a non‑creature artifact) that is put into its owner’s graveyard from the battlefield isn’t described by the term “dies.”

Related note: an object that is both an artifact and a creature (for example, an artifact creature) is a creature as well as an artifact, so it can “die” if it’s put into a graveyard from the battlefield (see [300.2]).

Assumption: I assume the question means a permanent that is an artifact but not also a creature or planeswalker. If the artifact is also a creature (an artifact creature), the answer is different as noted above.

results.question: what happens if i should draw a card when my library is empty?
results.text:
Direct answer: If you attempt to draw a card when your library is empty, you have attempted to draw from an empty library and you lose the game the next time a player would receive priority (a state-based action). 

Definition of “draw”: Drawing a card means putting the top card of a player’s library into that player’s hand ([Draw]; [121.1]). Because your library has no cards, the game treats that as an attempted draw from an empty library and the loss happens at the next state-based-action check ([121.4]; [704.5b]).

Other important points and exceptions (all of these can change or clarify that outcome):
- Replacement effects that replace a draw are applied even if no cards could be drawn; such a replacement effect can therefore apply in this situation and change what happens ([121.6a]; [614.11]).
- If an effect offers you the choice to draw a card while your library is empty, you may choose to do so (you still would be attempting to draw) unless some effect says you can’t draw cards, in which case you can’t choose to draw ([121.3]; [121.3a]).
- If an effect moves cards from your library to your hand without using the word “draw,” that isn’t a draw and thus doesn’t cause the loss-from-empty-library rule to apply; similarly, effects that move as many cards as possible from a library do as much as possible if fewer cards exist ([121.5]; [609.3]).
- If you are required to draw more cards than remain in your library, you draw the remaining cards and then lose the game the next time priority would be received ([104.3c]).

Assumption: I’m answering under the rules supplied above; these statements come from those rules and apply regardless of player count unless other rules (not provided here) say otherwise.

results.question: what are the steps in combat and when do I have priority as the defending player?
results.text:
Direct answer: The combat phase has five steps — beginning of combat, declare attackers, declare blockers, combat damage, and end of combat — and several step-begin turn-based actions happen immediately as those steps begin (so you cannot act during those turn-based actions). results.question: can i respond to a mana ability?
results.text:
No. You can’t “respond” to a mana ability: mana abilities don’t use the stack and resolve immediately when activated, so you can’t cast a spell or activate a (non-mana) ability in response to them ([605.3b], [405.6c], [605.4a]).

Definitions and short explanation:
- A mana ability is a (some) activated or triggered ability that could add mana to a player’s mana pool when it resolves and that otherwise meets the criteria in rule [605.1] (see the activated-ability specifics in [605.1a]); some activated and some triggered abilities can be mana abilities ([113.4], [605.1], [605.1a]).
- “Respond” means casting an instant or activating an activated ability while another spell or ability is already on the stack ([117.7]). Because mana abilities don’t go on the stack and resolve immediately after they’re activated, they can’t be targeted, countered, or otherwise responded to ([605.3b], [605.4a], [405.6c]).

Practical note: you can activate your own mana abilities whenever you have priority (and in certain special moments listed by the rules), so you can activate mana abilities before an opponent activates theirs if you have priority, but once an opponent begins to activate a mana ability you cannot “respond” to that activation ([605.3a], [117.1d], [405.6c]).

results.question: can you explain layers?
results.text:
Layers are the game's system for deciding the order in which continuous effects are applied to objects; they’re applied in a fixed sequence, with sublayers and timestamp/dependency rules used to order effects that belong to the same layer, and the result is recalculated continually and instantaneously.

Definition and basic procedure
- “Layer” — a system used to determine in which order continuous effects are applied [Layer].
- To determine an object’s characteristics you start with the object’s actual values (for a card, the printed values; for a token or copy, the values that created it), then apply all applicable continuous effects in a series of layers in order [613.1].

Which layers are mentioned in the provided rules
- Layer 1: rules and effects that modify copiable values are applied (see 613.1a). Within Layer 1 there are sublayers (for example, Layer 1a for copiable effects) and those sublayers are applied in a specific order; within each sublayer effects are applied in timestamp order unless dependency changes the order [613.2a][613.2].
- Layer 3: text-changing effects are applied (see 613.1c and see rule 612 for what a text-changing effect is) [613.1c][612.1].
- Layer 4: type-changing effects are applied (see 613.1d) [613.1d].
- Layer 5: color-changing effects are applied (see 613.1e) [613.1e].
- Layer 7: power/toughness effects are applied; Layer 7 is divided into sublayers and those sublayers are applied in order, and within each sublayer effects are applied in timestamp order unless dependency changes the order [613.4].

Ordering within a layer or sublayer
- Normally effects in the same layer or sublayer are applied in timestamp order: earlier timestamps are applied before later ones [613.7].
- If a dependency exists between effects in the same layer or sublayer, the dependency system overrides timestamp order and determines the order instead [613.8].

Other important points
- The application of continuous effects via the layer system is performed continually and automatically by the game, and all resulting changes to an object’s characteristics take effect instantaneously when the layer system is applied (they don’t wait for something else to “resolve”) [613.5].
- If a single effect has parts that belong in different layers (for example, an effect that changes color and gives +1/+1), each part is applied in its appropriate layer; if the effect begins applying in one layer it will continue to be applied to the same set of objects in each other applicable layer even if the ability that generated the effect is later removed while the layer processing continues [613.6].

Examples from the provided rules (showing how layers work in practice)
- Honor of the Pure and Gray Ogre: A 2/2 Gray Ogre under your control that becomes white (a Layer 5 change) then gets +1/+1 from Honor of the Pure (a Layer 7c effect), becoming 3/3; if it later becomes red, the Layer 5 change removes the color and Honor of the Pure no longer applies and the creature would revert to 2/2 [613.5].
- Act of Treason: its “Gain control of target creature until end of turn” part is a control-changing effect applied in Layer 2, and its “it gains haste until end of turn” part is an ability-adding effect applied in Layer 6; each part is applied in its respective layer [613.6].
- Svogthos, the Restless Tomb: an effect that first makes a land a creature (layers 4 and 7b) and then another effect that changes its type, color, and power/toughness (layers 4, 5, and 7b) shows that the same permanent is considered through each relevant layer and sublayer so interacting effects resolve to a final characteristic set across layers [613.6].

results.question: how does the legend rule work?
results.text:
Direct answer: If a single player controls two or more legendary permanents that share the exact same name, that player chooses one of those permanents to keep and the rest are put into their owners’ graveyards. This state-based action is called the “legend rule.”

Explanation and key terms
- “Legend rule” (a state-based action): when two or more legendary permanents with the same name are controlled by the same player, that player chooses one to remain and the others are put into their owners’ graveyards. See rule [704.5j].
- “Legendary” (the supertype): any permanent that has the legendary supertype is subject to the legend rule. See rules [205.4d] and [Legendary].
- Tokens named in a create instruction that are given a legendary name are created with that name and are therefore subject to the legend rule in the same way as non-token permanents. See rule [111.9] together with [704.5j].
- Planeswalkers that have the legendary supertype are also subject to the legend rule (this includes planeswalker cards that were given the legendary supertype by errata). See rule [306.4] together with [704.5j].

Practical notes
- The player who controls the duplicates chooses which one to keep; the ones not chosen are put into their owners’ graveyards (they don’t necessarily go to the controller’s graveyard if ownership differs). See [704.5j].
- The legend rule is a state-based action (not a triggered ability); it is applied automatically when state-based actions are checked. See [704.5j].

Assumptions and scope
- This answer uses only the provided rules text. I assumed the question concerns permanents on the battlefield (the zone addressed by the legend rule in [704.5j]); the provided context does not describe any special exceptions beyond what’s quoted.

Cited rules: [704.5j], [205.4d], [111.9], [306.4], [Legendary].

results.question: when does my creature die after its been marked with a lethal amount of damage?
results.text:
Direct answer: Your creature is destroyed as a state‑based action the next time state‑based actions are checked after the lethal damage is marked — in practice, that means it’s destroyed immediately before a player would receive priority (and right after damage is processed); regeneration can replace that destruction. 

Definitions and reasoning:
- "Lethal damage" means an amount of damage marked on a creature that is greater than or equal to that creature’s toughness (i.e., damage ≥ toughness). [120.6]
- Damage dealt to a creature (by a source without wither or infect) is marked on that creature. If the total marked damage is greater than or equal to its toughness, the creature has been dealt lethal damage. [120.3] [120.6]
- Damage itself doesn’t directly destroy the creature; instead, state‑based actions (SBAs) are what put a creature with lethal damage into its owner’s graveyard. [120.5] [704.5g]
- State‑based actions happen automatically whenever their conditions are met and they don’t use the stack. [704.1] They are checked any time a player would get priority; the game performs all applicable SBAs before priority is given. [117.5] Therefore, after damage is dealt and processed, SBAs are checked and the creature is destroyed immediately if it has lethal damage. [120.4c] [117.5]
- Combat damage is dealt simultaneously during the combat damage step; after that damage is dealt, the usual SBA check that will destroy creatures with lethal damage happens before players receive priority. [703.4m] [117.5]
- Damage marked on a permanent remains until the cleanup step (or it’s removed by regeneration); note that cleanup’s removal of damage happens much later and does not prevent the SBA that destroys a creature with lethal damage from occurring earlier. [120.6] [514.2]

Assumptions: This answer applies the normal priority/SBA rules used in both two‑player and multiplayer games; the timing for SBAs (checked whenever a player would get priority) is the same in multiplayer, so the practical outcome is the same. If you meant a very unusual timing (for example, asking whether the creature dies before some simultaneously resolving replacement effect), state that exact timing and I’ll analyze that specific ordering.

Short note on regeneration: If an effect regenerates the creature in response to the lethal damage (or replaces the destruction event), that regeneration replaces the destruction. [704.5g]

results.question: can I cast my commander from exile?
results.text:
Short answer: Usually no—you can’t cast your commander from exile unless an effect specifically lets you cast spells from exile. If your commander was put into exile since the last time state-based actions were checked, you may instead move that card to the command zone and then cast it from the command zone (paying the commander tax). 

Why: • “Cast” is the process of taking a card from where it is, putting it on the stack, and paying its costs (see rules 601.2b and 601.2f). A player may begin to cast a spell only if a rule or effect allows them to cast it (601.3f). • There is no general rule that lets players cast cards from exile; you can do so only if a specific rule or effect says so (examples in the provided rules: a plotted card may be cast from exile without paying its mana cost (702.170d); a card exiled via Adventure can be played from exile while it remains exiled (715.3d); some effects allow casting certain face-down exiled cards but only if you may look at them and the resulting spell matches the required qualities (406.3b and 601.3f)). • In the Commander variant, if a commander is in exile and that object was put into exile since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put that object into the command zone as a state-based action (903.9a; state-based actions defined in 704.1). If you put the commander card into the command zone, you may cast it from the command zone (903.8), subject to the additional {2} commander tax for each previous time you cast it from the command zone that game (903.8). • The rules also define what “a commander” is for these purposes: a legendary card designated as the deck’s commander; references to casting a commander refer to a spell that is a commander and references to a commander in a zone refer to the card in that zone that is a commander (903.3d). 

Assumptions and timing notes: • I assume you mean a normal commander card that was put into exile. If the commander was put into exile since the last time state-based actions were checked, you get the state-based-action option to move it to the command zone (903.9a); if it was put into exile earlier (i.e., not since the last SBA check), that opportunity already occurred and you can’t retroactively take it. • If a special card or effect in your game explicitly says you may cast that commander from exile (for example, a plotted-card effect or a specific effect granting permission to cast from exile), follow that effect instead (702.170d, 715.3d, 406.3b, 601.3f). 

Practical outcomes: • If no effect lets you cast it from exile and you don’t put it into the command zone via the state-based-action option, you can’t cast the commander from exile. • If you move the commander to the command zone under 903.9a, you may cast it from the command zone using 903.8 (commander tax applies).

results.question: what happens during the cleanup step?
results.text:
Direct answer: During the cleanup step the active player first discards down to their maximum hand size (if necessary), then all damage is removed from permanents and all “until end of turn” and “this turn” effects end. Normally no player receives priority during the cleanup step, but if any state-based actions would be performed and/or any triggered abilities are waiting to be put onto the stack, those state-based actions are performed and those triggered abilities are put onto the stack; then the active player gets priority and players may cast spells and activate abilities. If no state-based actions are performed and no triggered abilities are waiting, the cleanup step ends immediately. As the step ends, effects that last until the end of that step or phase expire and any unspent mana in players’ mana pools empties.

Reasoning and definitions (rules quoted by number):
- “Cleanup step” definition: the cleanup step is the second and final step of the ending phase (see rule 512.1). 
- Discard to maximum hand size is the first turn-based action of the cleanup step (see rule 514.1 and rule 703.4n). Immediately after that discard, the game proceeds to the next turn-based action (see rule 703.4p). 
- All damage is removed from permanents (including phased-out permanents) and all “until end of turn” and “this turn” effects end as the next turn‑based action; these happen simultaneously and don’t use the stack (see rule 514.2 and rule 703.4p). Note that damage remains marked on creatures until the cleanup step (see rule 120.6). 
- Priority during cleanup: normally no player receives priority during the cleanup step (see rule 514.3). The exception is that the game checks for state-based actions and waiting triggered abilities; if any are present, state-based actions are performed, the triggered abilities are put on the stack, then the active player gets priority and players may act (see rule 514.3a and rule 704.3). Once the stack is empty and all players pass in succession, another cleanup step begins (see rule 514.3a). If no state-based actions are performed on the first check and no triggered abilities are waiting, then no player gets priority and the step ends (see rule 704.3). 
- As the step ends, effects that last until the end of that step or phase expire and all unspent mana in players’ mana pools empties (see rule 500.5). Also, a step that gives no players priority ends when all specified actions that take place during that step are completed (see rule 500.3). 
- Special-case: if an effect “ends the turn,” follow the special ordering in rules 724.1d and 724.1f; in particular, if an effect ends the turn during the cleanup step, a new cleanup step begins (see rule 724.1d), and when an effect ends the turn the process gives no player priority while it runs but any triggered abilities that have triggered since that process began are put onto the stack during the cleanup step and then the active player gets priority (see rule 724.1f). 

Assumptions and scope: I used only the provided rules. This description is the game-wide procedure; the provided rules do not state any different multiplayer treatment, so this applies regardless of player count unless another rule outside the provided context says otherwise.

results.question: when are state-based actions checked?
results.text: Direct answer: State-based actions are checked any time a player would receive priority — which includes after turn-based actions that occur when a step or phase begins or ends — and during the cleanup step with the special handling described there. State-based actions are game actions that happen automatically (they don’t use the stack) whenever their listed conditions are met; they are not controlled by any player and are performed before that player gets priority. When a check for state-based actions happens, all applicable state-based actions are performed simultaneously as a single event; if any were performed, the game repeats the check until none are performed, and only then are triggered abilities waiting to be put on the stack placed on the stack and priority finally given. Special cases: when a step or phase begins, turn-based actions are dealt with first and then state-based actions are checked; during the cleanup step there’s an exception that can allow players to get priority after state-based actions and triggered abilities are handled; and when an effect ends the combat phase, state-based actions are checked with no player getting priority at that moment. (Definitions and sources: state-based actions are automatic game actions that don’t use the stack and happen whenever listed conditions are met.)

results.question: how do I know who the active player is?
results.text:
Direct answer: The active player is the player whose turn it is. (That is the definition of “active player.”) [102.1]

What that means in practice
- The active player is simply the player whose turn it currently is; look to the turn order to see whose turn it is. [102.1]
- In games using the shared team turns option, the team whose turn it is is the active team (so refer to that team for turn-based rights). [805.4a]
- If a player is being controlled by another player, that doesn’t change who is the active player; control of a player only changes who makes decisions for that player, it doesn’t change whose turn it is. [723.3]
- When multiple players must make simultaneous choices, the active player makes their choice first under APNAP order. [101.4]
- The active player is the player who gets priority to act (cast spells, activate abilities, etc.) when priority is determined. [117.1] The rules also note the active player gets priority at the normal priority timing points. [508.2]
- During the combat phase, the active player is the attacking player. In a two-player game, the nonactive player is the defending player. [506.2]
- If a game variant could result in more than one “active player” being relevant for an effect that says “the active player,” the controller of that ability chooses which active player it refers to when the effect is applied. [805.9]

Assumptions and scope
- I’m assuming you’re asking in the context of the core turn/priority rules given above; if you meant a different variant not covered by the supplied rules, say so and I’ll note any missing rules.

Concise takeaway: whoever’s turn it is is the active player; use the turn order, and apply the team and control rules above when those options are in effect. [102.1] [805.4a] [723.3] [101.4] [117.1] [508.2] [506.2] [805.9]

results.question: when someone other than the active player casts a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text: The player who cast the spell (the nonactive player) gets priority first — they keep priority immediately after casting the spell. Definition: “Priority” is the game rule that determines who may cast spells, activate abilities, or take special actions at a given time [117.1]. Reasoning: If a player has priority when they cast a spell, that player receives priority afterward [117.3c]. Also, if the nonactive player cast the spell in response to another spell or ability, the newly cast spell is considered to be cast “in response” and will resolve first [117.7].

results.question: when the active player cast a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text: The active player gets priority first after casting a spell. Priority is the right to cast spells, activate abilities, and take special actions (rule 117.1). Rule 117.3c says that if a player has priority when they cast a spell, that player receives priority afterward; because the active player must have had priority to cast the spell, the active player gets priority back first. (If the spell was cast while another spell or ability was already on the stack, that new spell is considered cast “in response” and will resolve before the earlier object, per rule 117.7.)

results.question: can I hold priority to cast more spells after I've cast one or more spells?
results.text:
Yes — if you had priority when you cast a spell, you get priority back afterward and may cast more spells (for example, to cast more instants in response). Definition: “priority” is the game state that lets a player cast spells, activate abilities, and take special actions (see rule [117.1]).

Why: Rule [117.3c] says that if a player has priority when they cast a spell, that player receives priority afterward. Rule [601.2i] restates that if the spell’s controller had priority before casting it, they get priority after it’s cast, so you can take further actions. Also, if you cast a spell while another object was already on the stack, that new spell is considered cast “in response” and will resolve first ([117.7]); the phase or step won’t end until the stack is empty and all players pass in succession ([500.2]), so players get chances to add more objects.

Exception/important special case: If you cast a spell because an effect specifically lets you cast it during the resolution of another spell or ability (that is, you’re casting “during resolution”), follow the casting steps but no player receives priority after it’s cast — so you cannot “hold” priority in that situation ([608.2g]).

Assumptions: I assume the cast was legal to begin with (no rule or effect prohibited casting). If the cast was illegal and later reversed, the player who had priority retains it per the illegal-action reversal rules ([733.2]).

results.question: when are lore counters put on sagas?
results.text:
Direct answer: Lore counters are put on Sagas when they enter the battlefield (via the Saga’s intrinsic “enters with” replacement ability) and again by a turn-based action immediately after a player’s precombat main phase begins (that player puts a lore counter on each Saga they control that has one or more chapter abilities). 

Short explanation and definitions:
- “Lore counters” are the counters Sagas use to track their progress. [714.3]
- Entering: Each Saga without read ahead has the intrinsic ability “This Saga enters with a lore counter on it,” and each Saga with read ahead has the intrinsic abilities that make it enter with the chosen number of lore counters. Those “enters with” and “as this enters” effects are replacement effects applied as the Saga enters the battlefield. [714.3a] [714.3b] [702.155b] [614.1c]
- Precombat main phase: Immediately after a player’s precombat main phase begins, that player puts a lore counter on each Saga they control with one or more chapter abilities. This is a turn-based action that doesn’t use the stack. [703.4f] [714.3c] [505.4]
- Related trigger note: Chapter abilities are triggered by “When one or more lore counters are put onto this Saga…” so both kinds of counter placement can cause chapter abilities to trigger (subject to read-ahead restrictions). [107.15a] [714.2b] [702.155a]

results.question: what is a delayed triggered ability?
results.text:
Direct answer: A delayed triggered ability is an ability that an effect creates during the resolution of a spell or ability (or when a replacement or certain static effects are applied) that will do something later instead of immediately; it will contain the words “when,” “whenever,” or “at,” and it does not trigger until it has actually been created. (See rules 603.7 and 603.7a.)

Key points from the rules (definitions and practical consequences):
- How it’s created: an effect creates a delayed triggered ability while a spell or ability resolves, as the result of a replacement effect being applied, or as the result of a static ability that allows a player to take an action (603.7a; 603.7; 608.3g; 610.2).
- Wording: a delayed triggered ability will contain “when,” “whenever,” or “at” (603.7; 603.7a).
- Timing of triggering: a delayed triggered ability won’t trigger until it has actually been created; if its trigger event already happened before it was created, it won’t trigger for that past event (603.7a).
- Frequency: a delayed triggered ability triggers only once—the next time its trigger event occurs—unless it has a stated duration (for example, “this turn”) (603.7b). If the trigger event happens multiple times simultaneously and the ability has no stated duration, the controller of the delayed triggered ability chooses which event causes it to trigger (603.7b).
- Source and controller: if a spell creates the delayed triggered ability, that delayed ability’s source is that spell and its controller is who controlled that spell as it resolved; if an activated/triggered ability creates it, its source is the same as that ability’s source and its controller is the player who controlled that ability as it resolved; if a static ability created it via a replacement effect or by allowing an action, the source/controller are determined as described in rules 603.7d–f and 603.7g (603.7d; 603.7e; 603.7f; 603.7g).
- Interactions with objects and zones: a delayed triggered ability that refers to a particular object still affects it even if the object’s characteristics change, but if that object is no longer in the zone the ability expects when the delayed ability resolves, the ability won’t affect it (603.7c).
- Special cases: a delayed triggered ability created by an ability that uses X will use the same X value as the creating spell or ability (107.3n). A delayed triggered ability that is created to trigger after an ability has resolved a certain number of times is created only once at the appropriate resolution (603.7h). Reflexive triggered abilities are treated as delayed triggered abilities that are checked immediately after they are created and trigger only if the specified action already happened during the resolution (603.12).

Assumption: I used only the numbered rules provided above; no outside rules were assumed.

results.question: can non-permanent spells have abilities?
results.text: Yes. Instants and sorceries (non‑permanent spells on the stack) can have abilities: those are called spell abilities and are followed as instructions while the instant or sorcery spell is resolving (spell ability). An “ability” is either a characteristic an object has that lets it affect the game, an activated or triggered ability that exists on the stack, or an ability granted to an object by an effect. Any text on an instant or sorcery is a spell ability unless that text is an activated ability, a triggered ability, or a static ability covered by the exception in rule 113.6. Abilities of instant and sorcery spells usually function only while that object is on the stack. Assumption: by “non‑permanent spells” you mean instant and sorcery spells on the stack; if you meant a different set of spells (for example, creature or artifact spells, which are spells but become permanents if they resolve), say so and I’ll restate under that assumption.

results.question: can I use a mana ability when a spell with split-second is on the stack?
results.text:
Yes. You can activate mana abilities while a spell with split second is on the stack. Split second is defined as “As long as this spell is on the stack, players can’t cast other spells or activate abilities that aren’t mana abilities” [702.61a], and the rules explicitly say players may activate mana abilities while a spell with split second is on the stack [702.61b].

A “mana ability” is a type of activated or triggered ability that follows the special rules for mana abilities [113.4][605.1]. Mana abilities don’t use the stack and can be activated at times other abilities often cannot (for example, whenever you have priority or while you are casting a spell or activating an ability that requires a mana payment) [117.1d][605.3a]. When a mana ability is activated it resolves immediately instead of going on the stack [605.3b][405.6c]; a triggered mana ability likewise resolves immediately after the mana ability that triggered it, without going on the stack [605.4a]. Also note you can only activate a mana ability if you can pay its costs (you can’t pay costs you don’t have the resources for) [118.3c], and once you begin activating a mana ability it can’t be activated again until it resolves [605.3c].

results.question: [Counterspell] is on top of the stack targeting my [Divination]. When everyone passes priority, what resolves first, and does Divination still resolve?
results.text:
Counterspell resolves first; when Counterspell resolves it “counters” Divination, so Divination does not resolve and is put into its owner’s graveyard.

Definitions and short explanation:
- “Resolve” — when the object on top of the stack resolves, its instructions are followed and it has its effect; when all players pass in succession the top object on the stack resolves (see rules 608.1 and 405.5). 112.1 explains that a spell is a card on the stack. 608.2n notes that as the final part of an instant or sorcery’s resolution, that spell is put into its owner’s graveyard.
- “Counter” — to counter a spell means to cancel it, removing it from the stack so it doesn’t resolve; a countered spell is put into its owner’s graveyard (see rule 701.6a).

Why this happens here: Counterspell is the topmost spell on the stack, so when all players pass it resolves first (405.5, 608.1, 117.4). Counterspell’s effect is “Counter target spell” (Counterspell card text), so as it resolves it removes the targeted Divination from the stack and puts Divination into its owner’s graveyard (701.6a). Because Divination was countered and removed from the stack, Divination does not later resolve. 608.2n describes that spells are put into their owners’ graveyards as part of resolution and 608.2b covers checking targets (not needed here because Divination is countered, not an illegal target).

Multiplayer note: The outcome is the same in multiplayer; if teams pass in succession the top object on the stack resolves first (805.5b).

Assumptions: I assume the timing you mean is ‘‘everyone passes priority with Counterspell on top of the stack targeting Divination,’’ as stated in the question. If instead Divination had already finished resolving before Counterspell was cast (a different timing), the answer would change — but under the stated timing Counterspell resolves first and Divination is countered.

results.question: My [Charging Rhino] has trample and is blocked by [Vampire Nighthawk], which has deathtouch. How much combat damage do I have to assign to the blocker before I can trample the rest over to the player?
results.text: Assign 1 damage from Charging Rhino to Vampire Nighthawk; the remaining 3 damage may be assigned to the defending player. Reasoning: Trample’s assignment step lets the controller assign lethal damage to blocking creatures first, then any excess to the player (see 702.19b). Deathtouch makes any nonzero amount of damage from the deathtouch source count as lethal for the purpose of determining excess damage (see 702.2c and 120.4a). Charging Rhino is a 4/4, so you can assign 1 to Vampire Nighthawk and assign the other 3 to the defending player, assuming Vampire Nighthawk has no damage already marked and no other creatures are assigning damage to Vampire Nighthawk this combat. If Vampire Nighthawk already had damage marked or other damage is being assigned to it this step, apply those amounts when determining what remains to be assigned (see 702.19b and 120.6).

results.question: I have [Monastery Swiftspear] on the battlefield and I cast [Shardless Agent]. When its cascade ability puts a noncreature spell onto the stack, does Monastery Swiftspear's prowess trigger before or after that cascaded spell resolves?
results.text:
Monastery Swiftspear’s prowess will trigger when you cast the spell chosen by Shardless Agent’s cascade, and that prowess trigger is put on the stack above that cascaded spell, so Monastery Swiftspear’s +1/+1 from prowess will resolve before the cascaded spell resolves.

When you cast that exiled spell, abilities that trigger when a spell is cast trigger then [601.2i]; Monastery Swiftspear’s prowess “goes on the stack on top of the spell that caused it to trigger. It will resolve before that spell” [Monastery Swiftspear ruling #2]. (If the cascaded spell is countered, Monastery Swiftspear’s prowess will still resolve after it has triggered [Monastery Swiftspear ruling #3].) This outcome is the same regardless of player count.
