results.question: My opponent's [Grizzly Bears] has 2 damage marked on it. Do state-based actions make it die before my [Lightning Bolt] resolves?
results.text:
Yes. Because Grizzly Bears already has damage marked equal to its toughness, state-based actions will destroy Grizzly Bears before Lightning Bolt resolves.

Reasoning and definitions: A state-based action is a game action that happens automatically whenever certain conditions are met; state-based actions don’t use the stack and are checked any time a player would get priority ([704.1], [405.6f], [117.5]). A creature that has total damage marked on it greater than or equal to its toughness has been dealt lethal damage and is destroyed as a state-based action ([302.7], [120.6]). Damage itself doesn’t “destroy” a creature directly; the creature is put into its owner’s graveyard by the resulting state-based action ([120.5]).

Application to this situation: Grizzly Bears is a 2/2 (card: Grizzly Bears) and already has 2 damage marked on it, which meets the lethal-damage condition ([302.7], [120.6]). State-based actions are checked before spells or abilities on the stack resolve (they are checked whenever priority would be given), so Grizzly Bears will be removed by state-based actions while Lightning Bolt (card: Lightning Bolt) is on the stack and before Lightning Bolt resolves ([117.5], [704.1]).

Assumptions and note: I assume the 2 damage is already marked on Grizzly Bears on the battlefield before Lightning Bolt resolves and you mean the ordinary priority window before resolution. If the 2 damage were only created during the resolution of a spell or ability, remember state-based actions aren’t checked during resolution (see [704.4])—that different timing can change the outcome.

results.question: It's my upkeep. My [Phyrexian Arena]'s beginning-of-upkeep trigger and my opponent's own beginning-of-upkeep trigger both want to go on the stack. Who chooses the order, and when exactly do they trigger?
results.text:
Direct answer: Both triggered abilities trigger when the upkeep begins. You (the active player) put all triggered abilities you control onto the stack first in any order, then your opponent puts all triggered abilities they control onto the stack in any order; because things placed later are higher on the stack, your opponent’s beginning-of-upkeep triggered ability will end up on top and resolve before Phyrexian Arena’s triggered ability. 

Why: A triggered ability is one written as “[When/Whenever/At] [trigger condition], [effect]” and has a trigger condition and an effect (definition: triggered ability) [603.1]. When the upkeep step begins, abilities that trigger “at the beginning of” that step trigger (they detect the event at the beginning of the upkeep) and will be put onto the stack the next time a player would receive priority [500.6],[603.2b]. The upkeep step has no turn-based actions and any abilities that triggered at the beginning of the upkeep are put onto the stack before the active player gets priority [503.1a],[117.3a].

If multiple triggered abilities have triggered since the last time a player received priority, they’re placed on the stack in a two-part APNAP process: first each player, in APNAP order, puts each triggered ability they control (that isn’t triggered by another ability) on the stack in any order they choose; then each player, in APNAP order, puts any remaining triggered abilities they control on the stack in any order they choose [603.3b]. In a two-player game the active player (you) is first in APNAP order, so you place Phyrexian Arena’s “At the beginning of your upkeep” triggered ability on the stack first in whatever order you choose, then your opponent places their triggered ability on top in whatever order they choose, so the opponent’s ability resolves first. 

Assumptions and multiplayer note: I assumed this is a normal two-player game and that your opponent controls a triggered ability that actually triggers at this upkeep (for example, an ability reading “At the beginning of each player’s upkeep…”). If this is a multiplayer or team game, apply team APNAP placement instead: members of the active team put their team’s triggered abilities on the stack first, then nonactive teams in turn order do the same [805.4d],[805.7]. If the opponent’s ability does not trigger on your upkeep (for example it reads “At the beginning of your upkeep” and its controller is your opponent), it wouldn’t trigger at your upkeep at all; I assumed the opponent’s trigger is one that does trigger on this upkeep.

results.question: I cast a sorcery with buyback and pay its buyback cost, then copy that spell with [Fork]. Once everything resolves, how many copies of the card end up back in my hand?
results.text:
One — only one card (the original sorcery card you cast with buyback paid) ends up back in your hand; the copy created by Fork does not return a card to your hand.

Reasoning and definitions
- Buyback: “Buyback [cost]” means “You may pay an additional [cost] as you cast this spell” and “If the buyback cost was paid, put this spell into its owner’s hand instead of into that player’s graveyard as it resolves.” This is a static ability that functions while the spell is on the stack [702.27a].
- Copy of a spell: To copy a spell means to put a copy of it onto the stack; a copy of a spell isn’t cast and has no spell card associated with it [707.10].
- Interaction here: You cast the original sorcery and paid its buyback cost, so as that original spell resolves its buyback returns that spell’s card to your hand instead of putting it into your graveyard [702.27a]. The copy Fork creates is a spell with no card object behind it, and a copied spell can’t return a card via buyback because there is no card to return [707.10]. The official Fork ruling states exactly that if you copy a spell for which Buyback has been paid, you get nothing back from the copy since the copied spell does not have a card to give you (only the original card returns) [Fork ruling #8]. Fork’s rulings also note the copy is not considered to have been cast and the copy on the stack has no card associated with it [Fork ruling #9][Fork ruling #10].

Assumptions
- I assume you cast the sorcery from your hand and paid its buyback cost when casting (as you stated). If you had cast the sorcery from a different zone where buyback doesn’t apply, the outcome could differ; the provided rules and rulings address the hand-cast, buyback-paid case described above.

results.question: I have a face-down manifested card that's really [Lightning Bolt]. It dies and I imprint it on [Mimic Vat]. Later I activate Mimic Vat's copy ability -- do I get a token?
results.text:
No — you won’t get a token. Lightning Bolt is an instant card; Mimic Vat may exile a manifested instant when it dies, but you can’t create a token that’s a copy of a nonpermanent card, so Mimic Vat’s activated ability won’t produce a token in that case.

Reasoning and assumptions:
- I assume “manifested” here means the card was a face-down manifested card that is actually Lightning Bolt (an instant). Lightning Bolt is a nonpermanent card (it’s an instant). (Card data: Lightning Bolt.)
- Mimic Vat’s imprint triggered ability can exile a manifested instant when it dies (Mimic Vat may exile that card). However, Mimic Vat’s activated ability can’t create a token that’s a copy of a nonpermanent card; if the exiled card is a nonpermanent card, no token is created. (Mimic Vat ruling #0.)
- You are still allowed to activate Mimic Vat’s activated ability even if no suitable card is exiled, but if the ability resolves and the only card exiled with Mimic Vat is a nonpermanent card like Lightning Bolt, no token is created. (Mimic Vat ruling #6 and Mimic Vat ruling #0.)

If you instead exiled a card that’s a creature card (a permanent card), Mimic Vat’s activated ability could create a token copy of that creature (subject to Mimic Vat ruling #4 about which card is exiled when the ability resolves).

results.question: My [Fiend Hunter]'s enters-the-battlefield ability is on the stack, about to exile a creature. I copy that ability with [Lithoform Engine] and target a second creature. Both get exiled. When Fiend Hunter later leaves the battlefield, do both come back?
results.text: Yes — both creatures exiled by the original Fiend Hunter’s enters-the-battlefield ability and the copy made by Lithoform Engine return to the battlefield when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield. Reasoning: Fiend Hunter’s printed abilities are a linked pair (one ability exiles a creature as it enters and the other refers to “the exiled card”), so the leave-the-battlefield ability refers to cards exiled by that enters-the-battlefield ability (see Fiend Hunter). Lithoform Engine ruling #4 explicitly says that if Fiend Hunter’s enters-the-battlefield ability is copied and two creatures are exiled, they both return when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield. The general definition of linked abilities explains that the second ability refers only to objects affected by the first ability ([607.1]), and rule [607.3] explains that when “the exiled card” is referenced but multiple cards were exiled, the reference applies to each of them. Assumption/timing note: I’m assuming Fiend Hunter remains on the battlefield until after both the original and copied enters-the-battlefield abilities have resolved and that Fiend Hunter later leaves the battlefield; if Fiend Hunter left before its original enters-the-battlefield ability resolved, Fiend Hunter ruling #0 describes a different outcome (the leave-the-battlefield ability would trigger and do nothing, then the enters-the-battlefield ability could exile a creature indefinitely).

results.question: My own [Banishing Light] has an opponent's creature exiled. On my opponent's turn I cast [Teferi's Protection], phasing out my Banishing Light. Does the exiled creature return to the battlefield?
results.text: No — the creature exiled by Banishing Light stays exiled; it does not return when Banishing Light phases out due to Teferi's Protection. Phasing means a permanent’s status becomes “phased out” (it’s treated as though it doesn’t exist) and phasing does not cause the permanent to leave the battlefield or change control. Banishing Light’s exile lasts “until this enchantment leaves the battlefield,” and phasing out Banishing Light isn’t the same as it leaving the battlefield, so that “until” condition is not met when Banishing Light phases out. Teferi's Protection’s ruling #21 explicitly states that one-shot effects waiting “until [this] leaves the battlefield,” such as that of Banishing Light, won’t happen when a permanent phases out. Therefore the exiled creature remains exiled; it will only return if and when Banishing Light actually leaves the battlefield (not when Banishing Light simply phases back in). Assumption: this is the usual two-player case; the same outcome applies here.

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. In response to its cast trigger, my opponent tries to [Counterspell] it. Can they even target it given protection from instants, and if it's countered, do I still control their next turn?
results.text:
Yes. Counterspell can target Emrakul, the Promised End while Emrakul, the Promised End is on the stack, because Emrakul, the Promised End’s protection from instants only applies while Emrakul, the Promised End is on the battlefield (Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #2; see also [702.16b]). If Counterspell resolves and counters Emrakul, the Promised End, the triggered ability created “When you cast Emrakul, the Promised End, you gain control of target opponent during that player's next turn. After that turn, that player takes an extra turn.” was already on the stack and can still resolve. Triggered abilities go on the stack when their trigger condition occurs ([603.1a]); triggered abilities on the stack aren’t spells and aren’t countered by spells that counter only spells ([113.9]). When the triggered ability resolves, the game checks whether its target(s) are still legal ([608.2b]); countering Emrakul, the Promised End does not by itself make the targeted opponent an illegal target, so the ability will give you control of that opponent during that player’s next turn and create the extra turn as written on Emrakul, the Promised End (assuming the targeted opponent remains a legal target). As part of Counterspell’s resolution, Emrakul, the Promised End (the spell) is put into its owner’s graveyard ([608.2n]).

Assumptions: two-player game and that the opponent cast Counterspell targeting the Emrakul, the Promised End spell on the stack in response to the triggered ability being created. If the triggered ability’s chosen target opponent later becomes an illegal target before that ability resolves, the ability won’t resolve ([608.2b]).

results.question: My cascade spell exiles cards until it hits [Valki, God of Lies], whose back face is the seven-mana planeswalker Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor. Is that a legal cascade hit, and can I cast the Tibalt side for free?
results.text:
Yes. Cascade can stop on Valki, God of Lies, and you may cast Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor (the back face) without paying its mana cost — provided the cascade spell’s mana value is greater than 2.

Why: Cascade is the triggered ability that exiles cards until you exile a nonland card whose mana value is less than the cascade spell’s mana value, and then lets you cast that exiled card without paying its mana cost if the resulting spell’s mana value is less than the cascade spell’s mana value [702.85a]. A double-faced card’s mana value is calculated using the mana cost of its front face (the card data for Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor shows MV 2, and the rules state a double-faced card’s mana value uses its front face’s cost) [712.8c]. Therefore the Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor card is a valid cascade hit when its printed/front-face mana value (2) is less than the cascade spell’s mana value, so cascade will stop there and offer you the cast option [702.85a][712.8c].

The ruling for that card makes the last step explicit for modal double-faced cards: if an effect lets you play or cast a card from among a group of cards, you may play or cast a modal double-faced card with any face that fits the effect’s criteria [Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16]. Cascade’s cast option is such an effect, and the face you choose to cast must meet the cascade requirement that the resulting spell’s mana value be less than the cascade spell’s mana value [702.85a][Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16]. Because the card’s mana value is 2 (the front face’s cost), casting the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor face is allowed as the “resulting spell” has mana value 2 for this purpose, so you may cast Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor without paying its mana cost if 2 is less than the cascade spell’s mana value [702.85a][712.8c][Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor].

Assumptions and notes:
- I assume the cascade spell’s mana value is greater than 2; if it is not, cascade wouldn’t stop on Valki, God of Lies because its mana value is 2 and cascade requires a strictly smaller value [702.85a].
- I relied on the card’s printed mana value and the double-faced-card mana-value rule; the answer would change if the provided context lacked those rules or the card’s MV. 

TL;DR: Yes — Valki, God of Lies is a legal cascade hit (MV 2), and you may cast Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor free as long as the cascade spell’s mana value is greater than 2.
citations: Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16
Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
results.text:
You will control one of your opponent’s turns (their next turn), you will get a second Emrakul, the Promised End as a token when the copied spell resolves, and copying Emrakul, the Promised End as a spell does not cause another “When you cast this spell” trigger. Because you copied the triggered ability as well as having the original trigger, you will create two separate “after that turn, that player takes an extra turn” effects; those two extra turns will both happen after the controlled next turn (the extra turn created last is taken first). The last-created control effect overwrites earlier control effects, so you only actually gain control for one of the player’s turns (the one targeted by the last-created control effect).

Reasoning and assumptions (two-player game assumed):
- A Lithoform Engine copy of the Emrakul, the Promised End triggered ability is a copy of that ability put onto the stack; a copy of an ability is itself an ability and can resolve to produce the same delayed effects as the original. (See 707.10; Lithoform Engine ruling #3.)
- A copy of Emrakul, the Promised End as a permanent spell is created on the stack by Lithoform Engine and, when that copy resolves, it becomes a token with the characteristics of Emrakul, the Promised End. Copies of spells are not cast, so creating that copy won’t cause any “When you cast this spell” triggers to be created. (See Lithoform Engine rulings #5 and #6; 111.13; 707.10.)
- Each time one of the Emrakul, the Promised End “When you cast this spell …” triggered abilities resolves, it creates the effects that (a) cause you to gain control of the targeted opponent during that player’s next turn and (b) cause that player to take an extra turn after that turn. Those created effects are delayed/ongoing effects produced by the resolving triggers. (See Emrakul, the Promised End card text and 603.7h.)
- If you create two such resolving triggered-ability results, both will create their extra-turn effects; rule and Oracle guidance say each ability’s effect will create an extra turn. (See Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14.) Per the extra-turn rule, if multiple extra turns are created, they are added one at a time and the most recently created extra turn is taken first. (See 500.7.)
- Multiple player-controlling effects that affect the same player overwrite each other; the last one created is the one that actually grants control during that player’s next turn. Therefore, although you produced two control effects by resolving two copies of the trigger, only the last-created control effect governs who controls that specific next turn. (See Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14.)

Timing assumption and how a different timing would change the result: I assumed you copied the triggered ability first (so the stack ends up with, top to bottom, the copy-of-spell, the copied trigger, the original trigger, then the original Emrakul spell). In that timing the copied trigger resolves before the original trigger, so the original trigger (resolving last) is the last-created control effect and therefore is the one that actually grants you control of the targeted player’s next turn. If instead the copied trigger were to resolve after the original trigger (so it is the last-created control effect), that copied trigger’s control effect would be the one that overwrote the earlier control effect; the high-level outcome remains: you get exactly one controlled next turn and two extra turns created, but which of your two created control effects wins depends on which triggered ability resolved last.

If you want the precise order the extra turns will be taken in your assumed timing: the extra turn created by the trigger that resolved last (the original trigger under my timing assumption) is the most recently created extra turn and so will be taken first, then the earlier-created extra turn is taken next. (See 500.7 and Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14.)

results.question: I've imprinted a creature on [Mimic Vat] and activate its ability to make a token copy. While that ability is on the stack, I copy it with [Lithoform Engine]. Do I get two tokens?
results.text:
Yes. You can get two tokens: the original Mimic Vat activated ability on the stack and the copy created by Lithoform Engine each resolve separately, and each can create a token copy of whatever card is exiled with Mimic Vat when that ability resolves. If no card is exiled with Mimic Vat at the time one of those abilities resolves, that resolving instance produces no token.

Why: Copying an ability puts a separate instance of that ability onto the stack (Lithoform Engine’s first ability does this) so you have two independent abilities to resolve ([Lithoform Engine ruling #3]; see the definition of copying an ability in rules [707.10e] and [707.10b]). The copied ability still refers to the same Mimic Vat as the original (a copy of an ability has the same source as the original, and “this [object]” refers to that same object) ([707.10b]; [201.5a]; [Lithoform Engine ruling #0]). Mimic Vat’s ability creates “a token that’s a copy of a card exiled with this artifact” when it resolves, and which card is copied is determined at resolution, so each resolving instance will create a token that’s a copy of whatever card is exiled with Mimic Vat at that moment ([Mimic Vat ruling #4]). You may activate and copy the ability even if no card is currently exiled; if none is exiled when a resolving instance resolves, no token is created for that instance ([Mimic Vat ruling #6]).

results.question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
results.text:
Direct answer: If you announce X = 0 for Awaken the Woods, you will pay {1}{G}{G} total and create 0 tokens — that is, you pay three mana (one of any color plus two green) and get nothing. Instead, you should choose X = 2 to get the best value: X = 2 also ends up costing {1}{G}{G} (three mana) but creates two 1/1 green Forest Dryad land creature tokens. 

Why (brief): Awaken the Woods has mana cost {X}{G}{G}, and you choose the value of X as part of casting the spell ([107.3a], [601.2b]). To determine what you actually pay, follow the ordering in rule and in Trinisphere’s ruling: start with the mana cost you’re paying (using the X you announced), apply any cost increases, then apply cost reductions, then apply Trinisphere’s effect if the mana component is less than three mana ([601.2f]; Trinisphere ruling #0). 

- For X = 0 the announced mana cost is {G}{G}. Your permanent’s {1} cost reduction can’t reduce any generic portion because there is no generic portion, so after reductions the mana component is still two mana ({G}{G}). Trinisphere then makes the spell cost three mana total, yielding a final cost of {1}{G}{G} per Trinisphere’s ruling; the spell’s effect creates X = 0 tokens (none). 
- For X = 1 the announced mana cost is {1}{G}{G}; the {1} reduction reduces the generic part to 0, leaving {G}{G}, and Trinisphere raises that to three mana => final cost {1}{G}{G}, producing one token. 
- For X = 2 the announced mana cost is {2}{G}{G}; the {1} reduction makes it {1}{G}{G} (total 3), and Trinisphere doesn’t change it because its mana component is already three — final cost {1}{G}{G}, producing two tokens. 

Thus X = 2 maximizes tokens you get for the same three-mana outlay; X ≥ 3 will raise the final total cost above three mana. 

Assumptions: I assume your unspecified permanent is a cost-reduction effect that reduces the generic portion of green spells by {1} as those reductions are applied while casting (not an alternative cost or replacement effect). I assume the table size (two-player vs multiplayer) doesn’t affect this cost calculation. If the permanent’s effect worked differently (for example, it set an alternative cost or reduced colored symbols), the result could change.

results.question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
results.text:
Yes. You can cast Animate Dead targeting Grist, the Hunger Tide in your graveyard; Animate Dead will return Grist, the Hunger Tide to the battlefield under your control, but Animate Dead won't end up attached to Grist, the Hunger Tide and Animate Dead will be put into your graveyard. The delayed triggered ability created by Animate Dead will trigger when Animate Dead leaves, but it will do nothing because Grist, the Hunger Tide is no longer a creature on the battlefield.

Why: Grist, the Hunger Tide is a creature card while it’s in your graveyard, so it is a legal target for Animate Dead’s “enchant creature card in a graveyard” (see Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1). Animate Dead’s enter-the-battlefield process returns the enchanted card to the battlefield and attempts to attach the Aura to that object (see Animate Dead ruling #1). When Grist, the Hunger Tide enters the battlefield it is no longer a creature and is just a planeswalker (see Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1), so Animate Dead “can’t legally be attached” as an Aura that enchants a creature. As explained by Animate Dead ruling #4, Animate Dead won’t be able to attach and is put into the graveyard as a state-based action; that causes Animate Dead’s delayed triggered ability to trigger, and when that trigger resolves “if the creature’s still on the battlefield, its controller will sacrifice it.” Because Grist, the Hunger Tide is a planeswalker on the battlefield (not a creature), the condition is false and no sacrifice occurs, so Grist, the Hunger Tide remains on the battlefield as a planeswalker under your control.

Assumption: I assumed a normal two-player game and standard timing for Animate Dead resolving; the provided rulings fully determine the interaction.

results.question: My commander [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] has four +1/+1 counters on it. It dies, I move it to the command zone, then recast it. Does it keep the counters, and does [Doubling Season] double them as it re-enters?
results.text:
Yes. Skullbriar, the Walking Grave keeps the four +1/+1 counters when it is moved to the command zone and when you recast it, and Doubling Season does not double those retained counters as it re-enters.

Reasoning and key definitions
- Definition: "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library" is a card-specific rule on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave that means Skullbriar’s counters persist with that object when it changes zones (this is an exception to the normal zone-change rule). See Skullbriar, the Walking Grave (card text and rulings).
- What happens when Skullbriar, the Walking Grave dies: In a Commander game, if Skullbriar, the Walking Grave is put into a graveyard, its owner may put it into the command zone instead (this is the Commander special action). Cite: 903.9a.
- Normal rule vs Skullbriar: Normally, an object that moves zones becomes a new object and its counters cease to exist (400.7; 122.2). Skullbriar, the Walking Grave’s printed text/rulings create an explicit exception: Skullbriar, the Walking Grave retains its counters as it changes zones (Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1 and #3). A card’s own printed text overrides the general rule when they conflict.
- Doubling Season interaction: Doubling Season affects counters that are put on a permanent or that affect permanents that enter with counters (Doubling Season ruling #2). However, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2 explicitly states that the counters that remain on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave as it changes zones aren’t "placed" on it and effects like Doubling Season won’t affect those retained counters. Therefore those retained +1/+1 counters are not doubled when Skullbriar, the Walking Grave re-enters the battlefield.

Assumptions
- You are playing a Commander game (you said "my commander"); the Commander-specific rules cited above apply. If you were not in a Commander game, the command-zone replacement/return rule (903.9a) would not apply.
- I assumed Doubling Season is on the battlefield in a position where it would normally affect counter-placement; Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2 still prevents Doubling Season from affecting the retained counters regardless.

results.question: I cast [Final Fortune] to take an extra turn. During that extra turn I use [Sundial of the Infinite] to end the turn before the end step. Do I still lose the game?
results.text: No. You don’t lose during that extra turn — activating Sundial of the Infinite to end the turn before the end step prevents Final Fortune’s “At the beginning of that turn’s end step, you lose the game” ability from triggering that turn; per Sundial of the Infinite’s ruling, that “at the beginning of the end step” trigger instead waits until the beginning of the next turn’s end step. Reasoning: Final Fortune’s lose condition is an “at the beginning of the end step”-triggered ability tied to the extra turn. Sundial of the Infinite’s ability ends the turn and skips to cleanup, and its ruling says any “at the beginning of the end step” triggered abilities won’t get the chance to trigger that turn and will trigger at the beginning of the end step of the next turn instead. (Final Fortune’s separate ruling that you don’t lose if the extra turn itself is skipped only applies when the extra turn is skipped outright; here only that turn’s end step was skipped.)

results.question: I cast [Clone]. When and how do I choose what it copies, and can my opponent respond to that choice?
results.text:
You choose what Clone copies as Clone enters the battlefield — that choice is made by Clone’s controller at the moment Clone would enter (it’s part of the “as … enters” copying process). Your opponent does not get a chance to respond to that choice itself, although your opponent can respond earlier while Clone is still a spell on the stack (for example, by removing the creature you might copy or by countering/destroying Clone before it resolves).

Reasoning and details
- Definition (key term): an “as this enters” choice is a choice made as the object is entering the battlefield as part of an effect that modifies the entering event; those choices are made by the entering permanent’s controller when the enter-as-thing replacement/continuous effect is applied, not later. [707.5],[707.6]
- When you choose: Clone’s ability (“You may have this creature enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield.”) is applied as Clone enters the battlefield, so Clone’s controller makes the copy choice at the moment Clone would enter. Clone becomes a copy as it enters (it doesn’t enter and then become a copy). [707.5],[707.6]
- What you may choose: you may choose any creature already on the battlefield (you may also choose not to copy). You can’t choose a creature that is entering simultaneously with Clone. [Clone ruling #2],[Clone ruling #5],[Clone ruling #0]
- Can an opponent respond to the choice itself?: No. The choice is part of the enter-as-a-copy event applied when Clone enters, so there is not a window after that choice in which players receive priority to respond to the choice itself. Opponents can, however, respond earlier while Clone is still a spell on the stack (before it resolves) — for example, by removing the creature you intended to copy or by otherwise changing the battlefield so that a different set of creatures is available when the enter-as-copy choice is made. If multiple replacement effects are trying to modify how Clone enters, the affected object’s controller chooses which replacement effect to apply. [616.1c]

Assumptions/disclosure
- I’m assuming a normal game where no additional, unlisted effects change when the choice must be made; if extra replacement effects that affect the entering event exist, apply rule [616.1c] as described above. If the game were multiplayer, the same timing applies because only Clone’s controller makes the enter-as-copy choice; simultaneous-choice APNAP rules (101.4) only apply if multiple players must make a choice at the same time.

results.question: I activate my [Flooded Strand]'s ability, then activate [Gogo, Master of Mimicry] with X=2 to copy it twice. How many lands do I get from that one Flooded Strand?
results.text:
You get three lands: one from the original Flooded Strand activation and one from each of the two copies that Gogo, Master of Mimicry created.

Reasoning: When you activated Flooded Strand’s ability you paid its costs (including {T}, paying 1 life, and sacrificing Flooded Strand) and put that activated ability onto the stack. Flooded Strand’s ability’s effect is to search your library for a Plains or Island card and put it onto the battlefield (see Flooded Strand). Gogo, Master of Mimicry’s ability with X=2 creates two additional instances (copies) of that activated ability on the stack (Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #6). A copy of an activated ability is put onto the stack (it isn’t activated) and is itself an ability on the stack; copies copy the characteristics and decisions of the original ability (707.10b). The copies’ source is the same as the original ability’s source (Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #9), so each instance on the stack will resolve and perform the same “search your library for a Plains or Island card, put it onto the battlefield, then shuffle” effect. Because the sacrifice was part of the cost you already paid for the original activation, that cost being paid doesn’t prevent the copies from resolving and producing their search/put effects (707.10b). Therefore you get three lands total (one per resolving instance).

Assumptions and timing note: I assumed you activated Flooded Strand’s ability and paid its costs (sacrificing Flooded Strand) before activating Gogo, Master of Mimicry and targeting that on-stack ability; that is the order stated in the question. If you hadn’t put Flooded Strand’s ability on the stack first, Gogo, Master of Mimicry couldn’t target it to copy it.
